content.value: A mixed fleet (tiny · lean · big) + a mixed batch routes so: the xl export takes the big box, the heavy cycle takes the mid box, light + standard pack onto the lean box — the big box spent only where it must be. The proof covers over-capacity (one placed, one honestly flagged), offline exclusion, fence non-co-location, over-budget refusal, and the spend cap.
python3 helpers/route.py
runs it.
Idle capacity is permission.
Free slots + budget headroom → the orchestrator raises ambition (bigger slices, deeper verification). Rising declines or failures → it narrows to small work. And the hard brake is one rule:
spend cap reached = ambition forced to zero
— every order refused until budget frees. That is the fleet-wide cycle brake, expressed as a routing fact, not a new mechanism.

blocks.text: Troubleshooting — the scars, so you skip them

items.label: Empty artifact
items.text: If an order keeps completing with no output, the worker delegated to a background task and ended its turn. Fix: enforce in-turn execution (the listener skill already does).

items.label: 409 forever
items.text: A fence held by a CLOSED order won't free (the known bug). Use unique fence strings per order; never reuse a fence across runs.

items.label: duplicate_task
items.text: Reusing an id or near-identical content across runs trips dedup. The bundled file-order.sh retries with the reported duplicate_of; prefix ids with a run tag.

items.label: Not claimable
items.text: A listener sees only its workspace/project/dataset. If orders never arrive, the listener and orchestrator are in different scopes — align with bp use.

items.label: priority rejected
items.text: Task priority must be 0-4; brief must be a blocks map, not a string. The helper handles both.

content.value: The strategy is fought and won. What remains is a short, safe build sequence.

Run a Fleet of Claude Codes

Barkpark · Personal Dev Fleet · Field guide · Rev 1 · 2026-07-21

One Claude Code conducts; others listen and work. Orders travel as tasks on the Barkpark ledger; fences keep them from colliding; the orchestrator routes each order to the cheapest box that can hold it. Works the same on your laptop and across cloud support servers — because the only thing that changes is where bp points. This is how to use it, proven end to end, with the safety rails that make it safe to leave running.

Two commands stand up a fleet: on the workers, “become a listener”; on the conductor, “orchestrate.” The ledger is the wire between them.

The mental model

A fleet is a conductor and its workers. The orchestrator turns a wish into small orders and hands them out. Each listener is a Claude Code that stays alive, waits for an order addressed to it, does the work itself, and reports back. There is no message bus to run: an order is an ordinary bp task, and the ledger is the wire.

Order= a task A bp task with an assignee (which listener), a brief (what to do + where to write), and one acceptance criterion. Nothing new to learn.
Doorbell= bp listen Listeners watch the live change feed and wake only when an order addressed to them appears. Idle costs nothing.
Scope= intrinsic Everything happens inside the active workspace / project / dataset. You never pass it; bp use sets it once.

Quickstart — locally

Three terminals on one machine. The fleet runs entirely against your local (or shared) ledger.

  1. Point every terminal at the same ledger

    bp use <server> — pick the Barkpark all fleet members share (local or cloud). bp use shows the active workspace / project / dataset; that scope is the fleet's world.

  2. Turn terminals 1 & 2 into listeners

    In each, run the fleet-listener skill: 'become a listener as support-1' (and support-2). Each announces its scope, arms the bp listen doorbell, and goes idle waiting for orders.

  3. Turn terminal 3 into the orchestrator

    Run the fleet-orchestrator skill, then hand it a wish: 'orchestrate: build X and verify it'. It decomposes into fence-disjoint orders, routes them to the free listeners, and tracks them.

  4. Watch the work land

    Listeners claim, work in-turn, stamp evidence, and close; the orchestrator grades the results honestly and reports. Then everyone returns to listening for the next wish.

The one-liner per role
/fleet-listener (in each worker terminal — name it) · /fleet-orchestrator (in the conductor terminal, then hand it a wish).

Quickstart — through the cloud

Identical, with one difference: the listeners run on cloud support servers instead of laptop terminals. This is the migration invariant — moving a worker to its own machine changes two things (the host it runs on, and the server bp targets) and zero lines of protocol.

See the fleetbp cloud status · the herdsame
Why the ledger-native design matters
Because orders route through the ledger by assignee — not through a local file or a socket — a listener on a cloud box and a listener in a laptop tab are the same to the orchestrator. That is what lets neighbour noise end at the machine boundary: a heavy job on a cloud support never touches your responsive local main.

PERSONAL DEV FLEET · THE FIELD GUIDE

Run a Fleet of Claude Codes

Barkpark · Personal Dev Fleet · Field guide · Rev 1 · 2026-07-21

One Claude Code conducts; others listen and work. Orders travel as tasks on the Barkpark ledger; fences keep them from colliding; the orchestrator routes each order to the cheapest box that can hold it. Works the same on your laptop and across cloud support servers — because the only thing that changes is where bp points. This is how to use it, proven end to end, with the safety rails that make it safe to leave running.

Two commands stand up a fleet: on the workers, “become a listener”; on the conductor, “orchestrate.” The ledger is the wire between them.

2+
Agents proven: Claude + Codex
1 cmd
To join the fleet
8/8
Router proof checks passing
~80%
CLI protocol already shipped
4
Resource size classes

Merge storms (fences hold)
§

  2. 2. Quickstart — locally
  3. 3. Quickstart — through the cloud
  4. 4. The two roles
  5. 5. Any agent, not just Claude
  6. 6. Efficiency: route by resource size
  7. 7. The safety rails
  8. 8. What is shipped, what is next
  9. 9. Troubleshooting
  10. 10. The perfect plan
§

The mental model

A fleet is a conductor and its workers. The orchestrator turns a wish into small orders and hands them out. Each listener is a Claude Code that stays alive, waits for an order addressed to it, does the work itself, and reports back. There is no message bus to run: an order is an ordinary bp task, and the ledger is the wire.

Order
= a task A bp task with an assignee (which listener), a brief (what to do + where to write), and one acceptance criterion. Nothing new to learn.
Doorbell
= bp listen Listeners watch the live change feed and wake only when an order addressed to them appears. Idle costs nothing.
Scope
= intrinsic Everything happens inside the active workspace / project / dataset. You never pass it; bp use sets it once.
§

Quickstart — locally

Three terminals on one machine. The fleet runs entirely against your local (or shared) ledger.

  1. Point every terminal at the same ledger

    bp use <server> — pick the Barkpark all fleet members share (local or cloud). bp use shows the active workspace / project / dataset; that scope is the fleet's world.

  2. Turn terminals 1 & 2 into listeners

    In each, run the fleet-listener skill: 'become a listener as support-1' (and support-2). Each announces its scope, arms the bp listen doorbell, and goes idle waiting for orders.

  3. Turn terminal 3 into the orchestrator

    Run the fleet-orchestrator skill, then hand it a wish: 'orchestrate: build X and verify it'. It decomposes into fence-disjoint orders, routes them to the free listeners, and tracks them.

  4. Watch the work land

    Listeners claim, work in-turn, stamp evidence, and close; the orchestrator grades the results honestly and reports. Then everyone returns to listening for the next wish.

The one-liner per role /fleet-listener (in each worker terminal — name it) · /fleet-orchestrator (in the conductor terminal, then hand it a wish).
§

Quickstart — through the cloud

Identical, with one difference: the listeners run on cloud support servers instead of laptop terminals. This is the migration invariant — moving a worker to its own machine changes two things (the host it runs on, and the server bp targets) and zero lines of protocol.

StepLocalCloud
Provision the boxyour laptopbp cloud instance create (a support server)
Authenticatealready logged inbp login + bp instance credentials <id>
Point at the ledgerbp use localbp use <main> — the main dev server
Become a listener/fleet-listenersame — /fleet-listener
See the fleetbp cloud status · the herdsame
Why the ledger-native design matters Because orders route through the ledger by assignee — not through a local file or a socket — a listener on a cloud box and a listener in a laptop tab are the same to the orchestrator. That is what lets neighbour noise end at the machine boundary: a heavy job on a cloud support never touches your responsive local main.
§

The two roles

The listener contract

source
Listen
bp listen — wake only on an order addressed to you
→
emit
Claim
bp task claim --resources <fence> — the claim IS the fence lease
→
emit
Work IN-TURN
do it yourself this turn; never background it and end the turn
→
emit
Stamp
bp task stamp — real evidence + the criterion verbatim
→
gate
Close
bp task close on the live epoch; return to listening

The orchestrator contract

source
Decompose
wish → small orders, one clear deliverable each
→
emit
Route
helpers/route.py — cheapest sufficient box per order
→
emit
Dispatch
file orders (assignee-routed) — the ledger delivers them
→
emit
Track
watch each order to done; a dark listener → reassign
→
gate
Grade
judge artifacts against sealed criteria — never rubber-stamp
The division of labour is absolute The orchestrator never executes order content and never claims a task; the listener never merges and never self-grades. For code, the orchestrator is the merge arbiter: workers leave PRs merge-ready, it merges serially, disarming collisions first.
§

Any agent, not just Claude

The fleet is provider-neutral by construction: it is built on bp and the ledger, not on anything one vendor owns. Any AI that can run a shell command OR speak MCP can be a worker. The only vendor-specific thing is how you launch one headless turn — a single adapter line.

AgentHeadless one-shot (the ONE provider-specific line))
Claude Codeclaude -p "$P" --dangerously-skip-permissions
OpenAI Codexcodex exec --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox "$P"
Anything elseFLEET_AGENT=custom FLEET_AGENT_EXEC='youragent {{PROMPT}}'
Proven live — Codex ran the full contract A real order routed to a Codex worker: it claimed with a fence, wrote the artifact, stamped evidence, and closed on the epoch — criteria 1/1, through the same ledger, with only the adapter line changed from Claude's. FLEET_AGENT=codex tooling/fleet/fleet-run.sh listen <name> and it joins the fleet.
CLI spine
bp Any agent with a shell tool runs the loop directly: bp task claim / pulse / stamp / close.
MCP spine
bp mcp serve Eight task tools over Model Context Protocol. Claude adds it as an MCP server; Codex: codex mcp add barkpark -- bp mcp serve.
Doorbell
bp listen A plain SSE stream any process consumes — no vendor SDK required.
§

Efficiency: route by resource size

A fleet is only efficient if a 32 GB export box is not wasted on a lint task and a lean box is never handed an export it cannot hold. The orchestrator gives every order a weight class and packs it onto the cheapest sufficient listener — best-fit-decreasing, capacity-, fence- and budget-aware.

ClassExample workWants a listener that is…
lightlint, a doc, a small editanything free — packs onto the smallest box
standarda feature slice, a reviewa lean box
heavyan epic-cycle wave, a builda mid/large box
xla full workspace export (~2.2 GB)a big box, run alone (SOLO)
Proven, not asserted — 8/8 router checks A mixed fleet (tiny · lean · big) + a mixed batch routes so: the xl export takes the big box, the heavy cycle takes the mid box, light + standard pack onto the lean box — the big box spent only where it must be. The proof covers over-capacity (one placed, one honestly flagged), offline exclusion, fence non-co-location, over-budget refusal, and the spend cap. python3 helpers/route.py runs it.

Idle capacity is permission. Free slots + budget headroom → the orchestrator raises ambition (bigger slices, deeper verification). Rising declines or failures → it narrows to small work. And the hard brake is one rule: spend cap reached = ambition forced to zero — every order refused until budget frees. That is the fleet-wide cycle brake, expressed as a routing fact, not a new mechanism.
